paragraphs: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning agent that learns a model and uses it to plan while selectively attending to parts of its current state. The central design question is how to keep planning focused on the objects that matter for solving a task. The agent is trained end to end, so this selective planning mechanism belongs to the learned system.

The state is represented as a set of entities. A bottleneck restricts how many entities the agent can attend to at each planning step, and the selection can change dynamically. This makes limited attention an explicit architectural constraint. Planning therefore operates through a small selection of relevant entities rather than requiring equal attention to the entire represented state.

The authors investigate this bottleneck in several collections of customized environments with different challenges. They consistently observe better generalization to compatible environments that were not seen during training. Their findings connect this improvement to attending to relevant objects, supporting selective attention as a useful design for transferring learned task-solving abilities within the tested settings.
neurips-2021-a-consciousness-inspired-pl.tldr: A planning agent that restricts attention to a few relevant entities shows better generalization to compatible unseen environments.

paragraphs: Temporal Graph Networks model graphs whose relationships change over time, but their complexity can also encourage fitting random noise. This paper tackles that problem through data augmentation with an adjustable strength. The aim is to vary training inputs enough to improve learning while preserving the information that gives the graph its meaning.

The proposed Memory Tower Augmentation module, called MeTA, processes graph augmentations at multiple levels. Each level handles a different augmentation magnitude, and messages pass between levels to provide adaptively augmented inputs for each prediction. The authors also introduce three augmentation strategies that alter temporal and topological features to model noise realistically. Together, these components make augmentation strength part of the prediction process.

MeTA can be incorporated into the training of popular temporal graph models without increasing their time complexity. Experiments on standard datasets show significant improvements in predicting edges and classifying nodes. These findings support using multiple interacting augmentation levels to improve the tested models efficiently, while addressing the risk that increased modeling capacity captures incidental noise.
neurips-2021-adaptive-data-augmentation-.tldr: MeTA adaptively combines temporal graph augmentations of different strengths to improve edge prediction and node classification efficiently.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a family of graph neural networks built from Beltrami flow, a diffusion equation defined for non-Euclidean geometry. The approach turns that mathematical evolution rule into a discrete neural computation. Its central idea is to let the representation of graph structure evolve together with the information attached to graph nodes.

Each node starts with its features plus positional encodings derived from the graph's topology. These encodings supply structural information alongside the node attributes. Beltrami flow jointly evolves both components, linking feature learning with topology evolution in one process. This coupling is the distinguishing architectural choice: the model's evolving representation includes information about both what nodes contain and how they are situated within the graph.

The authors state that this construction generalizes many popular graph neural networks, placing them within a broader diffusion-based framework. They also report state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. The contribution thus combines a mathematical organizing principle for graph architectures with empirical evidence that joint evolution of features and structural information can support strong predictive performance.
neurips-2021-beltrami-flow-and-neural-di.tldr: Beltrami-flow graph networks jointly evolve node features and structural encodings, generalizing existing architectures and achieving strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Physical simulations often represent continuous equations on irregular meshes. Neural models of these simulations can miss important relationships when they simply combine physical and mesh-related inputs into one feature vector. This paper proposes encoding those relationships directly into the network through conditional parameterization, making the architecture aware of information used by discretized numerical methods.

The method uses trainable functions of selected input parameters to generate neural network weights. Those parameters can include physical quantities and features of mesh topology. Consequently, the way a network processes modeled features depends explicitly on relevant physical or geometric information. The authors extend this idea flexibly across different network architectures, rather than tying it to a single simulation task.

Applications include discovering unmodeled physics, increasing the resolution of coarse fields, and simulating unsteady reacting flows. The conditionally parameterized networks outperform their traditional counterparts in the reported results. The paper also introduces CP-GNet, which can train on very few snapshots and is presented as the first deep learning model capable of standalone reacting-flow prediction on irregular meshes.
neurips-2021-conditionally-parameterized.tldr: Networks whose weights depend on physical and mesh information improve scientific modeling, including reacting-flow prediction on irregular meshes.

paragraphs: Scientific datasets can contain many measured variables, only some of which reveal useful patterns. This paper develops a way to select features without labels and demonstrates its value for clustering. The method combines a graph-based feature score with learned gates that suppress nuisance variables, allowing selection to be optimized through a differentiable objective.

The score uses a graph Laplacian and favors low-frequency features, meaning features that vary smoothly over the graph. A crucial choice is to compute this graph-based quantity using gated inputs. Otherwise, nuisance features can influence the very structure used to judge which features are meaningful. The gates are learned through continuous relaxations of Bernoulli variables, making feature inclusion amenable to gradient-based optimization.

The authors mathematically motivate the approach and show that constructing the Laplacian from gated inputs is crucial in a high-noise regime. Several real-world examples demonstrate advantages over leading baselines. The findings emphasize that feature selection and the graph used to assess features should be considered together when irrelevant measurements strongly affect the data representation.
neurips-2021-differentiable-unsupervised.tldr: Learned feature gates improve unsupervised selection by keeping nuisance variables out of the graph structure used to score features.

paragraphs: Learning hidden factors from observations is more useful when the model can identify those factors in a principled way. This paper introduces Structured Nonlinear Independent Component Analysis, or SNICA, as a framework for such disentanglement. Its contribution centers on extending identifiability theory for deep generative models to a broad class of structured data models.

Earlier results covered particular kinds of time-series models. SNICA's theorems extend the treatment to more general temporal structure and to richer dependencies, including spatial ones. A central result establishes identifiability within the framework even when observations contain noise whose distribution is unknown. This expands the theoretical setting in which hidden structure can be recovered without specifying the noise distribution beforehand.

To illustrate the framework, the authors introduce a nonlinear ICA time-series model that combines several capabilities. It handles both changing statistical behavior over time and temporal correlation in a fully unsupervised setting, reduces dimensionality, and models hidden states. Variational maximum-likelihood methods provide estimation and inference. This example shows how the broader identifiability framework can support multiple modeling requirements within one construction.
neurips-2021-disentangling-identifiable-.tldr: SNICA extends identifiable nonlinear latent-variable modeling to richer temporal and spatial structures, including noise with an unknown distribution.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn more than a single expected return. Distributional methods model uncertainty in returns, while hybrid reward architectures maintain separate values for different reward sources. This paper combines these ideas through Multi-Dimensional Distributional DQN, or MD3QN, which learns the joint distribution of returns across multiple reward sources.

Modeling the joint distribution preserves information about how reward uncertainties relate to one another. Separate return distributions describe variability within each source, but the joint model can also capture correlations across sources. The authors prove convergence of the joint distributional Bellman operator. Their practical algorithm learns by minimizing Maximum Mean Discrepancy between its predicted joint distribution and the corresponding Bellman target.

Experiments show that MD3QN accurately models joint returns in environments with strongly correlated reward functions. In control experiments, it also outperforms previous reinforcement learning methods using multidimensional rewards. The findings support treating relationships among reward sources as useful learning information, while the operator result supplies a theoretical foundation for extending distributional reinforcement learning beyond a single reward dimension.
neurips-2021-distributional-reinforcemen.tldr: MD3QN learns joint return distributions across reward sources, capturing their correlations and improving control in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a given rank-d matrix as the product of two factors, each with d columns. The objective measures the squared reconstruction error. Although this problem has a simple form, optimizing the factors is nonconvex, and unequal magnitudes between them complicate the analysis. It also serves as a prototype for matrix sensing and matrix completion.

Empirically, randomly initialized gradient descent has been observed to solve this factorization problem in polynomial time. Previous theoretical explanations required modifying the algorithm, for example by injecting noise during optimization or adding a regularizer to balance the two factors. The authors provide the first proof of polynomial-rate convergence to a global minimum for randomly initialized gradient descent on the stated asymmetric factorization problem.

The proof introduces a symmetrization technique that tracks both symmetry and asymmetry, alongside quantitative perturbation analysis for approximating matrix derivatives. These tools explain the behavior of the unmodified algorithm in this setting. The authors also suggest that the techniques may be useful for related nonconvex problems, presenting that broader applicability as a possibility.
neurips-2021-global-convergence-of-gradi.tldr: The paper proves polynomial-rate global convergence of randomly initialized gradient descent for the stated asymmetric low-rank matrix factorization problem.

paragraphs: Researchers compare neural network representations to understand what different models learn, but common comparison measures can disagree even on basic questions. For example, they can give conflicting accounts of whether changing only random initialization produces similar representations. This paper asks how those measures should be assessed when their answers do not agree.

The proposed framework connects representation differences to functional behavior. A useful measure should respond when a change affects what a network does, and remain insensitive when the change does not affect that behavior. The authors operationalize these requirements through statistical testing, examining behaviors such as probing accuracy and robustness under distribution shift. They study changes including random initialization and removal of principal components.

The analysis finds different weaknesses in existing metrics, including widely used approaches such as canonical correlation analysis and centered kernel alignment. A classical baseline performs surprisingly well, while some settings appear to defeat every examined metric. Those settings form a challenge set for improvement. The contribution is a behavior-grounded way to evaluate similarity measures, alongside evidence that current measures have distinct failure modes.
neurips-2021-grounding-representation-si.tldr: A statistical testing framework evaluates representation metrics by whether they detect behavior-changing differences and ignore behavior-preserving ones.

paragraphs: Score-based diffusion models generate data by reversing a stochastic process that gradually turns data into noise. Their usual training objective combines score-matching losses with chosen weights. Although a connection to continuous normalizing flows makes likelihood computation tractable, that does not mean the usual training loss directly optimizes likelihood. This paper addresses that mismatch.

The authors identify a weighting scheme for which the training objective upper-bounds negative log-likelihood. Minimizing this bound enables approximate maximum-likelihood training within the score-based diffusion framework. The distinction matters: the result supplies a mathematically justified objective connected to likelihood, while retaining the qualification that optimization proceeds through a bound rather than directly minimizing the exact negative log-likelihood.

Across multiple datasets, stochastic processes, and architectures, the authors empirically observe consistent likelihood improvements. Their best models obtain 2.83 bits per dimension on CIFAR-10 and 3.76 on ImageNet at 32 by 32 resolution, without data augmentation. These results are comparable to state-of-the-art autoregressive models on those tasks, showing that the revised weighting can make diffusion models competitive on this likelihood-based evaluation.
neurips-2021-maximum-likelihood-training.tldr: A particular score-matching weighting enables approximate maximum-likelihood training and consistently improves diffusion-model likelihoods in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Flood simulations depend on accurate terrain elevations because the shape of the ground influences water flow. Solving the underlying physical equations over a fine grid can be too expensive at large scales. Using a coarser terrain map reduces the computational burden, but may erase details that matter for the resulting flood prediction.

This paper trains a neural network to produce coarse terrain maps with the simulation outcome in mind. The training objective asks the flood prediction on the coarse representation to match the solution obtained on a fine grid. This makes downsampling sensitive to the physical task: the quality of the reduced map is judged through the water-flow prediction it supports.

The authors construct a dataset specifically for this learning problem and demonstrate that their method can substantially reduce computational cost while maintaining an accurate solution. The result supports learning the terrain representation as a way to make physical flood simulation more scalable. A reference implementation, together with documentation and dataset-reproduction code, accompanies the paper.
neurips-2021-physics-aware-downsampling-.tldr: A neural network learns coarse terrain maps that preserve fine-grid flood predictions while reducing simulation cost.

paragraphs: Interactive coding assignments, such as games, involve behavior that unfolds through user actions and changing internal states. This paper treats automated feedback for such programs as a problem of classifying Markov decision processes. Each student's program defines an environment, and the system must decide whether its dynamics and reward behavior should be categorized as correct or broken.

The proposed method, Play to Grade, combines an agent with an autoregressive model through a cooperative objective. The agent interacts with the submitted program to collect differential trajectories: sequences of behavior that help a classifier distinguish the relevant categories. This connects the choice of interactions to the grading decision, so the system gathers behavioral evidence by playing the program.

The authors demonstrate that this design enables automatic feedback for interactive code assignments. They also release 711,274 anonymized student submissions with manually assigned bug labels. All submissions come from a single assignment, giving the research community a large dataset within that particular educational setting. The contribution combines a formal view of interactive grading with a method for collecting evidence and a resource for further study.
neurips-2021-play-to-grade-testing-codin.tldr: Play to Grade learns to interact with student programs and use their resulting behavior to classify them as correct or broken.

paragraphs: Dense conditional random fields model dependencies among predictions, making their inference procedure an important part of the overall system. This paper introduces regularized Frank-Wolfe as a general approach to both inference and learning in these models. It works with a continuous, nonconvex relaxation of the original inference problem.

The algorithm uses ordinary Frank-Wolfe with approximate updates that are equivalent to minimizing a regularized energy function. This perspective encompasses existing approaches, including mean field and the concave-convex procedure. It therefore provides a common basis for analyzing methods that might otherwise appear separate. It also offers a straightforward route to exploring alternative regularized variants that could perform better.

Experiments on standard semantic segmentation datasets show that several variants outperform mean field inference. The gains appear both when the inference algorithm is used independently and when it is incorporated as an end-to-end trainable neural network layer. Dense CRFs using the new algorithms also significantly improve on strong convolutional network baselines. These results give practical support to the broader optimization framework and its flexibility.
neurips-2021-regularized-frank-wolfe-for.tldr: Regularized Frank-Wolfe unifies dense-CRF inference methods and yields variants that improve semantic segmentation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Q-learning can overestimate how valuable actions are, and this paper investigates that problem in cooperative multi-agent learning. The authors empirically find that QMIX suffers from more severe overestimation than previously recognized. They also find that existing approaches do not adequately mitigate it, motivating changes to the way joint action values are updated.

Their method combines two mechanisms. A regularized update penalizes large joint action values when they deviate from a baseline, helping stabilize learning. A softmax operator further reduces potential overestimation bias. Because applying that operator in a multi-agent setting presents computational challenges, the authors introduce an efficient approximation. Together, these components form Regularized Softmax Deep Multi-Agent Q-Learning, or RES.

RES is designed to apply generally to Q-learning-based multi-agent algorithms. The reported evaluation applies it to QMIX, where it avoids severe overestimation and significantly improves performance. Results reach the state of the art across several cooperative tasks, including StarCraft II micromanagement. The evidence links improved value estimation to stronger learning performance in these tested cooperative environments.
neurips-2021-regularized-softmax-deep-mu.tldr: RES combines value regularization with an efficiently approximated softmax operator to reduce QMIX overestimation and improve cooperative multi-agent performance.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates collecting experience from choosing an objective. An agent first explores without receiving rewards, then uses those samples to plan once a reward function is supplied. This paper studies that setting for episodic environments under a Linear Mixture MDP assumption: transition probabilities have a linear parameterization over features of states, actions, and next states.

The proposed UCRL-RFE algorithm has a provable exploration requirement for learning an epsilon-optimal policy for an arbitrary reward function. Ignoring logarithmic factors, its upper bound is H^5 d^2 / epsilon^2 episodes, where H is episode length and d is feature dimension. A variant using a Bernstein-type bonus improves this bound to H^4 d(H+d) / epsilon^2.

The authors also construct environments showing that any reward-free algorithm needs at least H^2 d / epsilon^2 episodes, up to logarithmic factors. Their upper bound matches this lower bound in its accuracy dependence and, when H is at least d, its feature-dimension dependence. These results characterize part of the exploration cost under the stated transition-model assumption without claiming that every dependence is optimal.
neurips-2021-reward-free-model-based-rei.tldr: UCRL-RFE provides sample-efficiency guarantees for exploring linear-mixture environments before a reward function is specified.

paragraphs: Causal learning can use data collected before and after an intervention, but the variables directly affected by the intervention may be unknown. This paper studies how to identify those targets in linear structural equation models with soft interventions. Existing approaches that require known targets or discover them through hypothesis testing can face substantial scaling and sample-efficiency difficulties.

The proposed algorithm estimates intervention sites from differences between the precision matrices of observational and interventional data. Precision matrices are inverse covariance matrices, so the method uses changes in statistical relationships among variables. It repeatedly performs this estimation on different variable subsets. This provides a route to target discovery that is organized around matrix differences.

The authors analytically establish consistency, sample complexity, and results concerning Markov equivalence. The algorithm can also refine an observational equivalence class of causal graphs into an interventional equivalence class. Simulations using real and synthetic data demonstrate gains for scalable causal structure recovery. Together, the findings support using the estimated intervention targets both as useful outputs and as information for narrowing the possible causal structures.
neurips-2021-scalable-intervention-targe.tldr: Differences between observational and interventional precision matrices enable scalable identification of soft-intervention targets in linear causal models.

paragraphs: Large language models often perform well despite having many more parameters than seem actively necessary for learning. Shapeshifter investigates whether the parameter matrices inside a Transformer can be represented much more compactly while retaining useful expressive power. It targets matrices in embedding, self-attention, and feed-forward layers, allowing compression to reach across the model.

The method first reshapes and rearranges an original matrix, then represents it through low-rank factors. This ordering is central to the proposed compact linear layers. The authors also prove that stacking these low-rank layers increases their expressiveness, providing a theoretical explanation for why a deep network can remain effective with this type of parameterization.

In the reported Transformer results, Shapeshifter reduces the total number of trainable parameters by more than a factor of ten, with little degradation on the original task. Each parameter matrix is replaced by a compact equivalent while the network architecture is maintained. The findings show that substantial parameter savings are possible through changes to matrix representation, supported by both expressiveness analysis and task-performance evidence.
neurips-2021-shapeshifter-a-parameter-ef.tldr: Shapeshifter compresses reshaped Transformer matrices into low-rank factors, reducing trainable parameters more than tenfold with little reported task-performance loss.

paragraphs: Sparse regression problems often require specialized optimization methods for different regularizers or constraints. This paper develops a more unified approach from iteratively reweighted least squares, or IRLS. A simple reparameterization, combined with a bilevel solution strategy instead of alternating optimization, turns the problem into minimizing a smooth function while retaining linear-system solves as its computational building blocks.

The resulting objective is nonconvex, but the authors establish favorable properties: it has no spurious minima, and its saddle points admit directions of descent. These results motivate using the BFGS quasi-Newton method. The approach aims to combine a simple solver with a formulation flexible enough to handle different kinds of sparsity and regularization strength.

Numerical benchmarks compare convergence speed with state-of-the-art solvers for Lasso, group Lasso, trace-norm regularization, and linearly constrained problems. The tested settings include hard constraints and design matrices ranging from correlated inputs to differential operators. The reported results show strong performance across this range, supporting the approach as a versatile alternative to choosing a different specialized solver for each problem.
neurips-2021-smooth-bilevel-programming-.tldr: A smooth bilevel reformulation of IRLS supports efficient optimization across several sparse regularizers and constrained regression settings.

paragraphs: Systematic generalization concerns applying learned knowledge to new combinations, a challenge for neural language models. This paper introduces the Edge Transformer to address that challenge using ideas from both Transformers and symbolic reasoning. Its architecture makes relationships between inputs a central part of the model's evolving representation.

The first change is to maintain a vector state for every pair of input nodes, representing an edge, instead of keeping states only for individual nodes. The second is triangular attention, which updates these pairwise representations through a mechanism inspired by unification in logic programming. Together, these choices give the model an explicit way to represent and update relations while drawing on a rule-based reasoning idea.

The authors evaluate compositional generalization in relational reasoning, semantic parsing, and dependency parsing. Edge Transformer outperforms relation-aware, Universal, and classical Transformer baselines in all three settings. These findings support the proposed combination of pairwise states and triangular attention on the examined benchmarks, providing evidence that architectural choices inspired by symbolic reasoning can help neural models handle new compositions.
neurips-2021-systematic-generalization-w.tldr: Edge Transformers combine pairwise representations with logic-inspired triangular attention to improve compositional generalization across three evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Writing deep learning programs imperatively in Python makes it easy to use ordinary programming features. Systems that convert these programs into optimized symbolic graphs can encounter unsupported operations, such as third-party library calls or dynamic control flow. Terra addresses this tension by combining imperative and symbolic execution within the same program.

Terra separates deep learning operations from Python features when building its symbolic graph. It then runs the Python portion imperatively while delegating the separated deep learning operations to symbolic execution. This division lets Python handle language features directly while the graph execution machinery optimizes the operations it receives. The system is presented as supporting arbitrary imperative deep learning programs through this co-execution design.

The authors evaluate coverage and performance on ten imperative programs spanning several neural network architectures. Terra speeds up all ten, whereas AutoGraph fails to execute five. These results demonstrate both execution coverage and performance benefits on the evaluated programs. They support co-execution as a practical way to preserve Python's usability while obtaining advantages from optimized graph execution.
neurips-2021-terra-imperative-symbolic-c.tldr: Terra jointly uses Python execution and optimized symbolic graphs, speeding up all ten tested programs while supporting features that block graph conversion.

paragraphs: Doubly robust estimation combines two quantities: a model of the conditional mean outcome and the logging policy, which gives the probability of selecting an action. This paper adapts that approach to experiments where data collection changes over time. Such adaptive experiments produce dependent samples, making their statistical analysis different from the independent-sample setting.

The authors propose adaptive-fitting, a variant of sample splitting, as part of their estimator construction. Its purpose is to obtain an asymptotically normal semiparametric estimator with dependent observations. Asymptotic normality provides a distributional characterization of estimation error as the sample grows, so the fitting procedure supports statistical analysis as well as the construction of an outcome estimate.

Simulations also reveal a surprising empirical pattern: the proposed estimator tends to perform better than other estimators that use the true logging policy. A related phenomenon is known for independent samples, but the authors explain that traditional arguments based on asymptotic efficiency do not account for their dependent-sample case. The reported advantage is an empirical tendency, rather than a universal claim that estimating a known policy always helps.
neurips-2021-the-adaptive-doubly-robust-.tldr: Adaptive-fitting supports doubly robust estimation with dependent experimental data and reveals an empirical advantage over some estimators using the true logging policy.

paragraphs: Language models can sometimes infer algorithmic patterns from a few examples, raising questions about which concepts they can learn and how many examples they need. This paper frames those questions as a teaching problem. The learner brings strong prior expectations, while a small witness set supplies examples intended to identify a particular simple algorithmic concept.

The study examines several GPT architectures alongside program induction systems and humans. It considers how behavior varies with concept complexity and with the number of additional examples. This comparison connects few-shot language-model behavior to machine teaching: the examples are studied in relation to the concept they are meant to communicate and the learner's existing preferences.

The broader question is whether learning from data can produce strong priors such as a preference for simpler explanations, associated with Occam's razor. Such preferences could help make learning from very few examples possible. The abstract presents this as an investigation and a joint analytical perspective; it does not state a definitive finding that language models have acquired that particular simplicity preference.
neurips-2021-think-big-teach-small-do-la.tldr: The paper studies few-shot algorithmic learning as machine teaching, comparing language models, program induction systems, and humans.

paragraphs: TransformerFusion reconstructs a three-dimensional scene from a monocular color video. A Transformer combines information from the video frames into a volumetric feature grid, which is then decoded into an implicit scene representation. The central task is to select useful visual evidence for each location in three-dimensional space.

The attention mechanism learns which frames are most relevant to each scene location using supervision from reconstruction alone. Features are combined from coarse to fine, and detailed features are stored only where needed. This reduces memory requirements and enables fusion at interactive rates. A multilayer perceptron then predicts surface occupancy from interpolated features across these levels to produce a higher-resolution reconstruction.

The reported results show accurate surfaces and improvements over state-of-the-art multi-view stereo depth estimation methods, fully convolutional reconstruction approaches, and recurrent video-fusion approaches using LSTMs or GRUs. These findings support attention as an effective mechanism for combining observations across frames. The coarse-to-fine representation also connects reconstruction detail to selective memory use, making efficiency part of the scene representation itself.
neurips-2021-transformerfusion-monocular.tldr: TransformerFusion attends to relevant video frames at each 3D location to reconstruct detailed scenes with selective fine-scale storage.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning commonly trains models through episodes, each representing a small task with limited labeled data. The choice of which episodes to present can shape what the model learns. This paper studies that sampling decision directly, asking how training should distribute its attention across tasks of different difficulty.

The authors first develop a method for approximating episode-sampling distributions in terms of difficulty. They then use it to compare sampling strategies. Their analysis finds that sampling uniformly over difficulty performs better than alternatives including curricula and schemes that emphasize easy or hard episodes. The relevant balance is across difficulty levels, so the method explicitly considers how challenging sampled tasks are.

Because the sampling approach is independent of a particular episodic learning algorithm, it can be used across different few-shot methods. Evaluations cover popular datasets, learning algorithms, network architectures, and protocols, demonstrating improved accuracy across the studied settings. The findings identify episode selection as a useful training choice in its own right and support balanced coverage of difficulty over the compared alternatives.
neurips-2021-uniform-sampling-over-episo.tldr: Sampling training episodes uniformly across difficulty improves few-shot learning over the compared curriculum and easy- or hard-focused strategies.

paragraphs: Real-world combinatorial decisions often involve uncertain objectives that must be understood from observations. A common strategy first learns the objective function and then optimizes it. This paper studies learning directly from input-solution pairs, aiming to predict high-quality combinatorial solutions without explicitly learning the objective function as an intermediate step.

USCO-Solver treats this task as regression between combinatorial spaces. Its proposed solver is designed for an abstract class of undetermined stochastic combinatorial optimization problems. To provide a learning foundation, the authors analyze learning error within the PAC-Bayesian framework using a new margin-based analysis. The theoretical contribution therefore concerns how learning from examples supports this direct solution-prediction formulation.

The empirical work consists of proof-of-concept experiments on several classic combinatorial problems using synthetic and real-world datasets. The authors compare the method with other potentially applicable approaches and report encouraging results. These experiments support the promise of the general solver design within the tested problems, while the abstract characterizes the experimental evidence as exploratory demonstrations rather than an across-the-board performance guarantee.
neurips-2021-usco-solver-solving-undeter.tldr: USCO-Solver learns combinatorial solutions directly from input-solution examples, supported by PAC-Bayesian analysis and encouraging proof-of-concept experiments.
